summary: This standards-track RFC defines a portion of the Management Information Base for managing Address Family Transition Routers (AFTRs) of Dual-Stack Lite.

eli5.summary: A set of dials and counters for watching the equipment that helps IPv4 traffic cross IPv6 networks.

subtitle: SNMP objects for watching and tuning the carrier-side router that carries IPv4 customers over an IPv6-only network.

tldr.problem: Dual-Stack Lite routers (AFTRs) combine an IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnel end with carrier-grade NAT, and the existing tunnel and NAT MIBs together cannot describe that combination.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7870 defines the DSLite-MIB module with a tunnel table, a NAT binding table that adds the tunnel's IPv6 address, alarm thresholds, per-subscriber statistics and three notifications.
tldr.outcome: Operators can configure and monitor an AFTR through SNMP. The module is rooted at mib-2 240 and adds a new tunnel type, dsLite(17).

today: RFC 7870 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2016, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the DSLite-MIB module.

sections.title: What the DS-Lite MIB Manages
sections.content:
Dual-Stack Lite (RFC 6333) gives customers IPv4 and IPv6 connectivity across an IPv6-only service provider network. Its two key parts are an IPv4-over-IPv6 tunnel and a carrier-grade IPv4-to-IPv4 NAT that shares the provider's IPv4 addresses among customers.

The device at the provider end is the Address Family Transition Router (AFTR). The customer side is the Basic Bridging BroadBand element (B4). RFC 7870 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for configuring and monitoring an AFTR.
sections.eli5: Some homes only have the new kind of road but still send old-style mail. The AFTR is the sorting centre that handles that, and this document lists the gauges to check on it.

sections.title: Framework and Relationship to the IF-MIB
sections.content:
The module follows the Internet-Standard Management Framework. MIB objects are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and defined with SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579, RFC 2580).

Under the Interfaces MIB (RFC 2863), each tunnel is a logical interface with an ifEntry, so each DS-Lite tunnel endpoint also has entries in the IP Tunnel MIB and the Interface MIB, indexed by ifIndex. The RFC maps interface objects like this:

  • ifOperStatus shows whether the DS-Lite tunnel function has been triggered.
  • ifInUcastPkts represents IPv4 packets encapsulated into IPv6 packets sent to a B4.
  • ifOutUcastPkts holds the IPv6 packets that can be decapsulated to IPv4 in the virtual interface.
  • ifMtu already carries the tunnel MTU, so this MIB defines none.
sections.eli5: Every tunnel already has a standard name tag and counters in the general interface list, so the new MIB reuses those instead of making its own.

sections.title: Why the IP Tunnel and NAT MIBs Are Not Enough
sections.content:
DS-Lite relies on IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnels and IPv4-to-IPv4 NAT. The NATV2-MIB (RFC 7659) can express IPv4-to-IPv4 translation, and the IP Tunnel MIB (RFC 4087) already supports IP-in-IP tunnels. Neither is sufficient alone, for two reasons.

  • Tunnel type. A DS-Lite tunnel is point-to-multipoint, but the direct(2) type in the IP Tunnel MIB only supports point-to-point. So tunnelIfEncapsMethod is set to the new value dsLite(17) and tunnelIfRemoteInetAddress must be ::.
  • NAT bindings. The AFTR is both tunnel concentrator and NAT. Returning IPv4 packets are matched in a NAT binding table extended with the tunnel initiator's IPv6 address (Section 6.6 of RFC 6333). The natv2PortMapTable is indexed by NAT instance, protocol, and external realm and address, while the tunnel table is indexed by ifIndex. A combined MIB is therefore necessary.

An implementation of the IP Tunnel MIB is required. The DS-Lite MIB supports only IP-in-IP encapsulation, since RFC 6333 defines no other types, and will be updated if others appear.
sections.eli5: One form tracks tunnels and another tracks address swapping, but the AFTR does both at once. This document stitches the two forms together so you can see which customer owns which swap.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB Module
sections.content:
The module is configurable per interface and depends on parts of the IF-MIB, IP Tunnel MIB and NATV2-MIB. Under dsliteMIBObjects are three subtrees:

  • dsliteTunnel: dsliteTunnelTable maps a B4 address to the associated AFTR address and can be used for row creation. Entries are indexed by address type (which MUST be ipv6(2)), start address, end address and ifIndex. The one readable object is dsliteTunnelStartAddPreLen, the prefix length of the initiator address. It exists because the address objects in the IP Tunnel MIB are not readable.
  • dsliteNAT: dsliteNATBindTable adds the B4's IPv6 address to the natv2PortMapTable. The external address type MUST be IPv4, and the internal address is the IPv6 tunnel source. Entries are lost upon agent restart.
  • dsliteInfo: alarm scalars and a statistics table.

For the NAT behaviours defined in RFC 4787, the mapping and filtering behaviour must be addressAndPortDependent(2) in DS-Lite. The address pooling object can be arbitrary(0) or paired(1).
sections.eli5: The control panel has three drawers: one for tunnels, one for the address-swapping list, and one for alarms and counters.

sections.title: Alarms, Statistics and Notifications
sections.content:
Three read-write scalars set alarm thresholds: dsliteAFTRAlarmConnectNumber (tunnels, range 60 to 90, default 60), dsliteAFTRAlarmSessionNumber (IPv4 sessions per user, default -1) and dsliteAFTRAlarmPortNumber (NAT ports used by a user, default -1). Other scalars carry the B4 address, protocol type (tcp, udp, icmp or total) and the specific IP address involved in an alarm.

dsliteStatisticsTable is indexed by subscriber and has 64-bit counters for discards, packets sent to and received from the subscriber, and current IPv4 and IPv6 sessions.

Three notifications exist. dsliteTunnelNumAlarm fires when the number of current tunnels exceeds the connection threshold. dsliteAFTRUserSessionNumAlarm fires when user sessions reach their threshold. dsliteAFTRPortUsageOfSpecificIpAlarm fires when the NAT ports used by a map address reach the threshold. A compliant agent must support the NAT bind, tunnel, statistics, notifications and alarm scalar groups.
sections.eli5: You can set limits, like a smoke alarm. If too many tunnels or too many ports are in use, the router sends a warning message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The three alarm threshold objects are read-write and so are sensitive. An attacker who sets a threshold very low can cause many useless notifications, and one who sets it very high can effectively disable notifications to hide another attack.

Readable objects can also be sensitive. Entries in dsliteTunnelTable reveal tunnel topology, and entries in dsliteNATBindTable can reveal the identity of private hosts in sessions with outside nodes, which would violate subscribers' privacy.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and deploying them is NOT RECOMMENDED. Implementations SHOULD provide the SNMPv3 security features. Those claiming SNMPv3 compliance MUST fully support authentication and privacy through the User-based Security Model with AES. Operators must configure access so only legitimate principals can read or change the objects.
sections.eli5: The dials and the list of who is talking to whom are private. Only trusted people should see or turn them.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA allocated the object identifier { mib-2 240 } to DSLite-MIB in the SMI Numbers registry, under the mib-2 branch (1.3.6.1.2.1). IANA also recorded the value dsLite(17), a DS-Lite tunnel, in the IANAtunnelType textual convention within the IANAifType-MIB.
sections.eli5: The module got its own official address, 240, in the big list of management objects, and the tunnels got the label 17.
